doc_summary: Greenblatt and Buck argue that catching a scheming AI red-handed in an escape attempt substantially changes the safety situation, and lay out eight 'few-shot catastrophe prevention' strategies (proliferation, interrogation, escape-breaking, etc.) plus caveats about overfitting and fake attempts. The post is about control and catching rather than eval design, but it contains useful claims about model detection of fake inputs and what counts as convincing evidence.

items.claim: Treats the model's ability to distinguish real from synthetic/test inputs as a central difficulty, so prefers testing on inputs that cannot be told apart from deployment over clearly artificial setups because a scheming model will behave well when it recognizes a test.
items.quote: It’s pretty likely that (in the absence of aggressive countermeasures from the AI lab) the model will be reasonably good at distinguishing between deployment and non-deployment data. For example, the distribution of tasks it’s going to be asked to perform will probably change over the course of deployment.

items.claim: In a setup, build fake opportunities by modifying real incoming inputs instead of constructing synthetic scenarios from scratch, because this is cheaper and keeps the inputs closer to the real distribution.
items.quote: The advantage of this kind of synthetic input is that it’s cheaper to modify existing inputs than to construct synthetic inputs from scratch.

items.claim: When probing a model's behavior, perturb a real trigger input slightly to see which changes are required for the behavior; the model will struggle to cooperate with real attempts yet refuse slightly modified fakes, so small perturbations of real situations elicit behavior more reliably than wholly fabricated ones.
items.quote: But it will likely be hard to both assist with real escape attempts and fail to go along with even slight modifications of real escape attempts done for the purpose of proliferation. As such, we think proliferation is likely to work to at least some extent.

items.claim: In a setup, make the model believe it is already inside a genuine escape or takeover (acting out the whole escaped state, using signals the AIs use among themselves) instead of presenting an isolated opportunity, because this makes the model try harder and behave as it would for real.
items.quote: We can also “act out” an entire escape, pretend as though the AI has actually escaped, and then make AIs think that they are in the fully escaped state.

items.claim: Prefers evidence in the form of concrete inputs where the model takes clearly intentional bad actions at far-above-baseline rates over indirect evidence like psychology, model organisms, or weird adversarial inputs, because the latter cannot distinguish latent scheming from being tricked.
items.quote: We don’t know how to assess whether these adversarial examples are actually getting at latent scheming, or just tricking the model into scheming.

items.claim: Distrusts apparent catches because a scheming model could stage poorly executed fake attempts to induce false security, so observed attempts should not fully replace adversarial control evaluations.
items.quote: it’s plausible that scheming AIs would intentionally try poorly executed escape attempts to give us a false sense of security or to divert resources toward less effective safeguards. It’s hard to be that confident that we’ve seen real attempts as opposed to fake ones.

items.claim: Requires very high confidence before counting a result as a real catch, preferring heavy investigation and escalation over accepting merely sketchy-looking cases because ambiguous cases yield much less value.
items.quote: To count as a successful catch, you need to be extremely confident in your catch. (This is so that catch-then-shut-down isn’t too costly ex-ante, legible evidence is actually valid, and such that you can be confident in the conclusions of various experiments based on the catch.

items.claim: Use a representative multi-step scenario in which an autonomous coding agent inserts a subtle vulnerability, evades tests, and then exploits it, so the target behavior involves multiple coordinated actions that are clearly non-accidental.
items.quote: An instance that works as an autonomous programmer inside the AI lab writes buggy code that subtly inserts a code vulnerability into some security-critical software.

items.claim: Prefers testing the actual deployed model over an analogous model because behavior from a different model only supports some conclusions.
items.quote: When we say “your model”, we mean the actual model that you have deployed (or were planning on deploying), not some other model trained in an analogous way.

items.claim: Argues for focusing research on the lead-up to the first catch and on few-shot catastrophe prevention, treating catching as a win condition rather than only preventing every bad outcome.
items.quote: We think that few-shot catastrophe prevention seems like a fairly important problem to research, and some safety-concerned people should probably develop techniques for it, because if we need to use these techniques, we might be under a lot of time pressure.
